title: Abu Sufyan and Hind
hook: leaders of Mecca's opposition, who became Muslim when Mecca opened

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khalid ibn al-Walid, who broke the lines at Uhud and later carried the banner. Your line was people change.

Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says it on the day Mecca opens, as Sahih Muslim records. A strange sentence, once you know whose house that was. At the end of Uhud, it was Abu Sufyan, leading the Meccan army, who called across the field: is Muhammad among the people? Is Abu Bakr? Is Umar? He cried out in praise of Hubal, the idol of Mecca, and the answer came back, as Sahih al-Bukhari records it: God is higher and more majestic. Now that same man's front door is named a refuge. Today: Abu Sufyan, and his wife Hind.
screen: `WHOEVER ENTERS HIS HOUSE IS SAFE.` → `IS MUHAMMAD AMONG THE PEOPLE?` → `GOD IS HIGHER.`

segments.voice: For years Abu Sufyan led Mecca's opposition to the Prophet. Hind, his wife, stood with him; the biographies tell hard stories of her at Uhud, around the death of the Prophet's uncle Hamzah. Then came the opening of Mecca, the conquest, when the Muslims entered the city and the enemy's house became a shelter. Abu Sufyan, the biographies say, became Muslim. Then Hind. Bukhari keeps her words, and they are startlingly honest. There was a time, she told the Prophet, when no household on the face of the earth was one I wanted humbled more than yours. Today, no household on the face of the earth is one I want honored more than yours. She didn't pretend the past away. She named it, then named the change. The Prophet answered with an oath of his own, by the One in whose hand is his soul. In the same report she goes straight on to a household problem: Abu Sufyan is tight with money; may she take what her children need? Yes, she's told, what is reasonable. From enemy of a house to ordinary questions within the community, in one conversation. They came late, after years of fighting, after Uhud and all it cost. Sunni tradition counts them among the companions. The door was not shut because they arrived at the end.
screen: `YEARS OF OPPOSITION.` · `THE ENEMY'S HOUSE, A SHELTER.` · `NO HOUSEHOLD I WANTED HUMBLED MORE.` · `NOW NONE I WANT HONORED MORE.` · then, large: `LATE, AND WELCOME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you once opposed, a rival, an old classmate, a relative you clashed with, and try Hind's two sentences quietly. Finish the first honestly, back then, I saw you as, and then the second, now, I see; if the second is hard to finish, that is worth knowing too. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Fath, the opening, the conquest of Mecca after which Abu Sufyan and Hind, once his fiercest opponents, became Muslim and were welcomed in. Today's word.
Your line: late, and welcome. Coming at the end still counts as coming. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 844 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IKRIMAH, SON OF ABU JAHL.`

notes: Hind at Uhud and the death of Hamzah: the sira's account (including mutilation) is only alluded to ('hard stories'); Keeper to confirm the level of detail.
'The Prophet answered her warmly': Bukhari 3825 has him reply 'and also, by Him in whose hand is my soul' (or similar); confirm the summary.
Abu Sufyan's conversion timing (just before the entry into Mecca) is from the sira; the script says 'he became Muslim' without detail.
Hook says 'a few years later': vague timing; confirm or cut.
Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm.
'The tradition remembers them anyway as companions' is a general claim; Sunni tradition counts both as companions; other views exist about Abu Sufyan. Keeper to decide whether to note this.
